# Lambda announces GPU price rises of about 15% — B200, H100 and A100 80GB, from Nov 16

Nov 6, 2026

Read on Lambda's own pricing page today, Nov 6, 2026: the Instances table now prints the prices that take effect on Nov 16, 2026 — HGX B200 up $1.00 an hour, H100 up $0.60 and A100 80GB up $0.40. It is the largest single announced rise we have caught this autumn, and renters have ten days' notice.

Image: GPUJournal price record — read on lambda.ai/pricing

What was announced, in the pricing page's own words (read Nov 6, 2026): 'These prices take effect November 16, 2026, at 00:00 UTC. Until then, log in to your Lambda Cloud account to see current pricing.' The printed Nov 16 rates: HGX B200 $7.69 an hour (from the $6.69 last verified on Nov 5, +14.9%), HGX H100 $4.59 (from $3.99, +15.0%), HGX A100 80GB $3.19 (from $2.79, +14.3%), and HGX A100 40GB unchanged at $1.99. Lambda is also now at a new address — lambda.com — announced on its blog on Nov 5, 2026; the pricing page itself still answers at lambda.ai/pricing.

How we are treating it: an announced rise is not a live price. Our board keeps Lambda's last verified rates until Nov 16 and will move only when the new rates are re-verified in effect on or after that date — the rise is recorded in Price Watch today as announced, with both dates. One consequence of the announcement is already live, though: Lambda's currently-effective rates can no longer be read on its public page, only after logging in, so today's public check could verify the future rates but not re-read the current ones.

results.title: Neocloud vs hyperscaler GPU: what capacity costs | Casitel
highlights:
# Neocloud or hyperscaler? What GPU capacity really costs.

Neocloud vs hyperscaler GPU rates for the H100, H200 and B200, read on 3 November 2026, with published commitment discounts and what else changes the bill.

C Compute · H100 list rates, per GPU-hour Rates read 3 November 2026

$3.99 lowest H100 rate in this note, at Lambda and E2E Networks

Each provider's own page, read 3 November 2026. Not executed prices.

Neocloud vs hyperscaler GPU pricing looks like a simple contest. The specialists charge less and the big clouds charge more. The rate cards say that is mostly true. They also leave out most of what you will pay and what you will get. This note sets out who sits on each side, what each publishes for the H100, H200 and B200, and what else moves the bill.

...

A neocloud is a cloud built around GPUs. Newcomer, writing in May 2026, names Lambda and Crusoe as neoclouds that own their chips and sell the compute. CoreWeave and Nebius are two more. Regional ones sit in other markets: E2E Networks in India and Sakura Internet in Japan both publish GPU rates and commitment terms.

...

## What the rate cards say

All rates below are US dollars per GPU-hour, taken from each provider's own page on 3 November 2026. They are list rates. They are not what large buyers sign.

Provider H100 H200 B200 What the rate is

Lambda$3.99 Not listed$6.69 On-demand, 8-GPU instance

E2E Networks$3.99$5.29$7.99 On-demand

Nebius$4.50$5.40$8.50 On-demand, HGX

CoreWeave$6.16$6.31$8.60 On-demand, North America

AWS$5.97$6.87$14.21 Capacity Blocks, a short reservation

Google Cloud$9.80$10.71 Not read Vertex AI, managed service

Oracle$10.00$10.00$14.00 Pay as you go

Microsoft Azure$12.29 Not read Not read ND H100 v5, East US

Three of these need a note. CoreWeave and Azure price a whole 8-GPU machine by the hour: $49.24 and $98.32 for the H100. The per-GPU figures above are our own arithmetic. AWS publishes a plain on-demand rate only in its calculator, so the AWS row is its Capacity Blocks price, and for the H200 it is the p5e machine (the p5en costs $7.90). Google's row is the Vertex AI managed service, which is not the same product as a bare virtual machine.

Even so, the spread is wide. The H100 runs from $3.99 to $12.29, about three times. The B200 runs from $6.69 to $14.21, about twice. Rate cards also move. In our read on 8 October, Nebius showed $3.85 for an H100. On 3 November it showed $4.50.

## What commitments change

Every provider here says a commitment lowers the rate. Few publish by how much.

C Compute · published commitment discounts Read 3 Nov 2026

E2E Networks 10% to 30%, its own figure

Sakura Internet 5% for 6 months, 10% for 12

Each provider's own pages, read 3 Nov 2026. Discounts off list rates.

- CoreWeave says it offers up to 60% off its on-demand prices for committed use. That is its own claim. The page lists no committed rate.
- Azure publishes reservation prices through its public price API. For the H100 machine in East US, the one-year price works out 36% below pay as you go and the three-year price 56% below. We divided each term price by its hours.
- Google Cloud lists Flexible Savings Plan rates on the Vertex AI page. For the H200 they are $9.64 for one year and $8.57 for three, which is 10% and 20% below $10.71.
- E2E Networks says three-month, six-month and annual commitments can earn 10% to 30%, depending on length and volume.
- Sakura Internet announced on 1 July 2026 a commitment plan for one H100 plan: 5% off for six months and 10% off for twelve.
- AWS cut P5 (H100) prices by 44% for on-demand and 45% for the three-year Instance Savings Plan from 1 June 2025. Those are cuts from its earlier prices, not discounts off today's rate.
- Nebius and Lambda name no percentage. Both point large buyers to sales.

The pattern is clear. The big clouds publish a formula. The neoclouds publish "up to" and a phone number. How GPU deals actually close covers what moves a private quote.

# Upcoming SaladCloud Price Changes: November 1, 2026

SaladCloud GPU pricing is changing on November 1, 2026: High, Medium, and Low Priority prices rise on 21 GPU classes. Lowest Priority is unchanged.

Jared Carpenter

Product Update SaladCloud Mon Oct 26 2026

We're raising GPU prices on SaladCloud where demand has outpaced supply. High, Medium, and Low Priority prices are going up on 21 GPU classes. Lowest Priority pricing is unchanged on every class.

These changes take effect Sunday, November 1, 2026 at 00:00 UTC, and they will impact active and running instances at that time.

## Summary Copy Anchor Link

- High Priority prices are increasing on 21 GPU classes, by 10% to 20% on most of them.
- Medium and Low Priority prices are increasing on the same 21 classes, by smaller amounts.
- Lowest Priority pricing is unchanged on every GPU class.
- Every GPU class not listed below is unchanged at every priority level.

...

Over the past several weeks, demand has outpaced supply on many of our most popular GPUs. Several classes have been running almost entirely at High Priority, and many of you have waited for capacity or not gotten it at all.

SaladCloud runs on GPUs that individuals share with the network, and those providers have other options. Paying them a competitive rate is how we keep the machines we have and bring new ones online, so alongside these price changes we're raising provider payouts to attract more supply.

The increases are also weighted toward High Priority. When nearly everything runs at High, priority stops meaning much. High rises the most, Medium and Low rise less, and Lowest stays the same, so the gap between tiers widens: High stays available for work that needs it, and the lower tiers have more room.

results.title: Nebius removes its spot-price ceiling — preemptible GPUs can now cost more than on-demand | GPUJournal
highlights:
# Nebius removes its spot-price ceiling — preemptible GPUs can now cost more than on-demand

Nov 2, 2026

In an update note dated Nov 2, 2026 on its own blog, Nebius says the cap that kept its dynamic spot price one cent below the on-demand rate is gone. Spot still has a floor — it just no longer has a top, and setting your own max price is now the only brake.

Image: Nebius via nebius.com

What changed, from Nebius's own post “Introducing spot pricing for preemptible VMs” (published Sep 22, 2026; read Nov 2, 2026): its update note, dated Nov 2, 2026, reads — “this section previously stated that the spot price always stays between a floor and a ceiling one cent below the on-demand rate. We have removed the ceiling. Customers can cap what they pay by setting a max price.” The post's how-it-works section now states plainly: “There is no upper limit, so during periods of high demand the spot price can rise above the on-demand GPU-hour rate.”

How the mechanism works, in the same post: the spot price for a GPU type in a region is set from available capacity and real-time demand, recalculated up to every 15 minutes, and it still cannot fall below a set floor — only the ceiling has gone. A renter who sets a max price keeps the old protection by hand: when spot rises above the cap, the instance stops, data is retained, and it can restart when the price falls back — automatically for Kubernetes clusters, manually (or via Terraform, SDK, API or CLI) for standalone VMs. A renter who instead chose to follow the spot price has no cap at all after today's change.

What did not change: Nebius's on-demand list. Re-read on Nebius's own prices page on Nov 2, 2026, B300 is $9.50 an hour, B200 $8.50, H200 $5.40, H100 $4.50, RTX PRO 6000 $1.80 and L40S from $1.55 — every figure the same as our Nov 1 read. This is not a price rise in the list; it is the removal of the guarantee that the interruptible lane is always the cheaper one.

...

### What it means if you rent GPUs

If you rent preemptible VMs on Nebius, do one thing today: set a max price. The ceiling that used to do that job for you was removed on Nov 2, and a workload set to follow the spot price can now be billed above the on-demand rate in a high-demand hour — paying a premium for capacity that can still be reclaimed. The discount lane still exists, but from today the discount is something you enforce yourself.

results.title: Nebius Group rolls out public live GPU spot pricing in Europe, adds reserve auctions and capacity rebates | The Apex Times
results.author: The Apex Times Newsroom
highlights:
Business/ The Apex Times/ Nov 3, 1:29 PM EST

# Nebius Group rolls out public live GPU spot pricing in Europe, adds reserve auctions and capacity rebates

The AI cloud provider says its new pricing and incentive programs aim to give developers more real-time cost visibility and reduce utilization risk for customers building on demand.

By The Apex Times Newsroom 2 min read AI-assisted Apex article

Nebius Group, a Nasdaq-listed operator of AI and cloud infrastructure, says it has launched public “live GPU spot pricing” for customers using its AI cloud services in Europe. The change is designed to make the cost of on-demand GPU capacity more transparent by tying pricing to real-time market conditions rather than fixed contract rates.

According to the announcement reported by Yahoo Finance, Nebius is also introducing additional marketplace mechanics, including reserve auctions. In practical terms, reserve auctions are meant to allow capacity procurement and pricing to balance supply and demand while still setting a floor for how capacity can be allocated, which Nebius frames as improving how customers access compute as their workloads fluctuate.

Alongside the pricing framework, Nebius unveiled what it describes as a capacity rebate program. The program is presented as an incentive that links customer economics to how capacity is used, with the company aiming to offset some of the financial uncertainty that can come with variable compute demand. The details provided in the report emphasize the existence of the rebate concept, but do not spell out the precise formula in the material available for this story.

results.title: The Compute Price Reset: Priced Like Credit - DalalBytes
results.author: Prakash Damodaran
highlights:
Spot and on-demand series followed the contract market up, with one pause in the summer. Silicon Data's neocloud H100 index, $2.37 per GPU-hour when it launched in May 2025, troughed at $2.00 in December 2025 and reached $2.82 on October 10, 2026, and $2.88 by October 24. JPMorgan put the average H100 on-demand rental in the non-hyperscale market at $2.68 per GPU-hour in July 2026, down 1.1% on the month and the first decline after seven consecutive increases, with utilization still above 70%. GetDeploying's median on-demand H100 rate across 41 providers was $3.50 in October 2026, about 13% above a year earlier. The H200 median rose about 26% over the same twelve months, to $4.70.

...

These are posted prices, the ones a new customer is quoted before any negotiation.

| Posted price increase | Was | Now | When |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lambda, H100 SXM on demand | $2.99 | $3.99 | June 2026 |
| Runpod Secure Cloud, H100 SXM | $3.29 | $3.99 | By October 2026 |
| Nebius, HGX H100 on demand | $3.85 | $4.50 | October 1, 2026 |
| Nebius, HGX B300 on demand | $7.85 | $9.50 | October 1, 2026 |
| AWS P5 Capacity Blocks, per H100 | $5.191 | $5.970 | August to October 2026 |

...

For most of this market, price is something a provider posts and a customer accepts. The exception of the year is Nebius, the neocloud that spent 2026 finding out what its capacity was actually worth, in public.

It started with an auction. Nebius disclosed its first capacity auction with its second-quarter 2026 results, and CEO Arkady Volozh described the outcome on the earnings call: "It was very successful and cleared at the highest price we have seen for the Blackwell generation of chips, 15% above the highest price we ever charged before. This gives us a strong signal on the value of this capacity in the market in real time." Chief revenue officer Marc Boroditsky added that the clearing price was 20% above the company's Blackwell pipeline pricing. The sequence matters. Nebius had already raised prices by hand, repeatedly, and demand had not blinked. The auction's message was that the manual increases had still been too small.

The posted prices followed. On October 1, 2026, Nebius raised on-demand rates by 17% to 21% across its NVIDIA line: the H100 from $3.85 to $4.50, the H200 from $4.50 to $5.40, the B200 from $7.15 to $8.50, and the B300 from $7.85 to $9.50. Its second-quarter shareholder letter had already reported pricing for older-generation GPUs running more than 30% above the first quarter. Management told investors it sold out of capacity as fast as new capacity came online, and that it could sell its 2027 capacity today at current deal terms but is holding some of it back for customers with immediate needs.

Then came the structural move. On October 8, 2026, Nebius switched its preemptible GPU capacity to dynamic spot pricing. The price is set per GPU type and per region from available capacity and demand, it can change as often as every 15 minutes, and it floats between a floor Nebius sets for each GPU type and a ceiling of the on-demand price minus $0.01. A customer either follows the spot price or sets a maximum price, and a machine whose cap is crossed stops. The prices are public without an account: seven days of history on the website and 30 days through the API.

Silicon Data sampled that API through the first nine days, October 8 to 16, and the newborn market behaved like a market. Nebius's H100 spot price sat at its $0.79 floor for most of the window, about two thirds below the $2.33 market spot median, and changed on only two of the eight measured days. Its H200, B200, and B300 prices moved on most days, mostly below market spot medians of $2.92, $4.01, and $4.95 respectively, and Nebius quoted below every other seller on most days for every GPU it lists. Set against the wider market, the contrast is sharp: more than half of all the spot price series Silicon Data tracks did not change once in the same nine days. Nebius is, so far, the only major seller whose prices actually float.

The industry's anchor used to run this experiment, and chose to stop. AWS built the original cloud spot market, then replaced its bid-driven pricing in November 2017 with a model that, in AWS's words, delivers prices that adjust gradually based on long-term trends in supply and demand. The spikes disappeared, and so did the information a floating price carries. AWS's accelerator capacity does reprice today, through Capacity Blocks, on a schedule measured in months; the current rates are next scheduled to update in January 2027. Nebius reprices in minutes and publishes the tape. In a shortage, that difference is worth money, and the auction measured how much: 15% above the best price the company's own sales process had ever achieved.

...

Accuracy. Compute price figures come from the trackers and providers named beside them: the SemiAnalysis one-year H100 rental index as reported; JPMorgan's July 2026 on-demand reading as reported; Silicon Data's neocloud rental indexes and its October 8 to 16, 2026 study of Nebius spot pricing; GetDeploying's provider medians; Ornn's transaction index; and provider price lists checked in October 2026, including AWS on-demand and Capacity Blocks pricing, Google Cloud TPU pricing, Azure and CoreWeave list prices, and the Lambda, Runpod, and Nebius price pages. Nebius auction and spot pricing details are from the company's second-quarter 2026 earnings call, its shareholder letter, and its published documentation, and the terms of its July 2026 secured facility are from company reporting of that closing. Amazon chip figures are from AWS pricing pages and company statements. Custom silicon share figures are broker and research-firm estimates as reported, including Bernstein's hyperscaler wallet framing and TrendForce shipment and packaging allocation data, and are estimates, not census counts. Intel figures are from Intel's third-quarter 2026 earnings release and guidance and from the DalalBytes Intel investment report. The credit tiering, cycle grading, and margin sequence readings are the author's analysis of the price data presented, not reported fact. The July 2018 Cloud TPU price cut is from Google Cloud's own release notes of that date. Prices in this market change often and by region and commitment; figures here are dated snapshots, not quotes. Errors can occur and facts change; verify independently before acting on anything you read.
